passages.original: Cujus quæstionis bealus Augustinus profunditatem sibi imperscrutabilem cernens, nullam voluit hujus rei definitam proferre sententiam , incongruum prorsus existimans aliquid affirmare sine dubitatione velle, quod alter posset contraria responsione convellere. Cujus tam in decimo libro de Genesi ad litteram, quam in libris ad Vincentium Victorem de Origine animæ, nec non in libro primo ex duobus quos ad sanctum Hieronymum scripsit (Epist. alias 28, nunc 166); in tribus quoque epistolis (V. epist. ejusd. alias 157, nunc 190) quas ad Optatum episcopum de hac quaestione composuit, disputatione refulget non minus copiosa quam profunda;
passages.english: Blessed Augustine, perceiving the depth of this question to be unsearchable to him, was unwilling to put forward any definite opinion on this matter, thinking it wholly unfitting to want to affirm without hesitation something that another could overturn with a contrary answer. Both in the tenth book on Genesis according to the letter, and in the books to Vincentius Victor on the Origin of the soul, and also in the first of the two books which he wrote to Saint Jerome (Epist. formerly 28, now 166), and in the three letters (see letters of the same, formerly 157, now 190) which he composed to Bishop Optatus on this question, his discussion shines out, no less copious than profound;
passages.notes: 'bealus' read as 'beatus'. 'Cujus ... disputatione' (whose discussion) rendered as 'his discussion'. The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: CAP. XXI.—33. His enim omissis, quas supra posuimus, catholicæ fidei veris manifestisque sententiis, in I diversos errores multi miserabiliter inciderunt. Tertullianus quippe animam non spiritum esse dicens. sed corpus, vehementer erravit, eo usque desipiens, ut etiam summum et verum Deum corpus esse diceret: cum non solum de Deo rerum omnium creatore legamus, quia Deus spiritus est (Joan. IV, 24), verum etiam de angelis quos Deus creavit, dicatur in psalmo : Qui facit angelos suos spiritus (Psal. CIII, 4). Animam quoque humanam spiritum rationalem esse nemo sapiens dubitet : de quo spiritu Apostolus dicit : Quit enim scit hominum quæ sunt hominis nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est (1 Cor. ii, 11) ? Ideo et sanctus evangelista rationalem animam, quam ChrisLus cum carne suscepit, non corpus, sed spiritum esse docuit. Nam ipse Salvalor dixerat : 497 Potestatem habeo ponendi animam meam, et potestatem habeo iterum sumendi eam (Joan. x, 18) : quam sine dubio tunc posuit, cum evangelista dicit, quia inclinato capite emisit spiritum (Joan. XIX, 30). Anima vero humana in eo rationalis ostenditur, in quo ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei facta narratur. passages.english: CHAP. XXI.—33. For when these true and manifest teachings of the catholic faith, which we set out above, were abandoned, many have wretchedly fallen into various errors. Tertullian, indeed, saying that the soul is not spirit but body, erred greatly, being so foolish as to say that even the supreme and true God is a body: whereas we read not only of God, the creator of all things, that God is spirit (John 4:24), but also of the angels whom God created it is said in the psalm: Who makes his angels spirits (Ps. 103:4). And let no wise person doubt that the human soul too is a rational spirit, of which spirit the Apostle says: For who among men knows the things that are of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? (1 Cor. 2:11). Therefore the holy evangelist too taught that the rational soul which Christ took up together with flesh is not a body but a spirit. For the Saviour himself had said: I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again (John 10:18); and this, without doubt, he laid down at the moment when the evangelist says that, having bowed his head, he gave up the spirit (John 19:30). The human soul, moreover, is shown to be rational in this, that it is recounted to have been made in the image and likeness of God. passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'in I diversos' (stray I), 'Quit' for 'Quis', 'ChrisLus', 'Salvalor', 'mulua' for 'mulus'. '497' is a page number, omitted. Psalm reference completes in following context (31:9). Latin 'anima' rendered 'soul' in John 10:18 to keep the argument; often translated 'life'.
